sentences.show: He had 37 wounds, and they zipped him into a body bag. He was still alive.
His name was Roy Benavidez, a Green Beret from Texas.
In Vietnam, in 1965, he stepped on a land mine. Doctors said he'd never walk again.
At night, against orders, he crawled out of bed and taught himself to stand.
He walked out of the hospital, and went straight back to Vietnam.
On 2 May 1968, a 12-man team was trapped by an enemy battalion.
Helicopters couldn't land. Benavidez jumped aboard one anyway.
He leapt out with a knife and a medical bag, and ran into the gunfire.
Shot in the leg, the face and the head, he kept dragging the wounded to the helicopter.
Then the pilot was killed, and it crashed.
He pulled the survivors out, and called in air strikes.
An enemy soldier clubbed him from behind. He fought him hand to hand, and won.
Six hours later, at least eight men were alive because of him.
Back at base, they thought he was dead. As the doctor zipped up the bag, Benavidez spat in his face.
For years, the Army refused him the Medal of Honor. There was no living witness.
Then his radioman, whom he believed dead, read about him in an Australian newspaper.
In 1981, President Reagan gave him the medal, and said: if this were a movie script, you would not believe it.
Roy never left a man behind. Don't leave this channel behind. Subscribe.
